transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you. Um... well, I'm here because I just can't seem to shake this feeling that work isn't safe anymore. And, I don't know, I feel like I'm somehow damaged now. It's like the competent person who used to do my job, the one who got promoted... she just isn't really there anymore.
Was there a particular event or incident at work that happened before you started feeling this way?

Yes, there was. Um, this has all been going on since a break-in that happened at the office. I was there doing an overnight deployment... and, yeah, that was about two years and four months ago now. Everything kind of started after that.
Since the break-in, have you had unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about that night that intrude on your thoughts?

Yeah, I do. It happens a lot when certain things set it off... like hearing a badge scanner beeping, or just heavy footsteps out in the hallway. Even getting a late-night deployment alert can do it. It suddenly puts me right back in that office. My chest gets really tight, and the image of the guard on the floor just... it cuts right through whatever I’m trying to do at the time.

Aside from those flashback moments, do you often feel detached from yourself or your surroundings—like you're observing yourself from outside your body, or like things around you feel unreal or dreamlike?

No, I don't think I've experienced that. I don't ever feel like I'm outside my body or anything, and things around me don't feel like a dream. 

If anything, it all feels a little too real. I just get stuck in those memories, but I'm definitely still in my own body when it happens.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient developed intrusive memories, physiological reactivity (chest tightness), and trauma-specific triggers (badge scanner beeping, footsteps, late-night alerts) following exposure to a life-threatening traumatic event (an armed break-in with an injured guard) at work approximately 28 months ago. Symptoms have persisted well beyond one month, confirming chronic PTSD rather than acute stress disorder. No dissociative depersonalization/derealization symptoms were endorsed, ruling out the dissociative subtype. The clinical picture is consistent with a specific, identifiable traumatic stressor causing re-experiencing symptoms with functional and psychological impact, fitting F43.1 (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder).
